Just finished my first playthrough and I can say I really liked the game and I think it totally worth the full price. The premise is original and simple (in a good way): check out an apparently missing person phone's and try to figure out what has happened to her.

In gameplay terms this translates to a visual novel+puzzle solving mash-up. Not that I considerer this a bad thing at all, quite the opossite I think it allows to put emphasis on a strong branching narrative.

I found it easy to "put myself in character" since the game revolves around interacting with the phone's apps and the story tackles on some contemporary problems -like whom you can trust on a social network, how much of info you should share, sexual harrasment, etc-. I know is not the first game that deals with many of these issues: I can recall Orwell but in that case the tone is more scify/conspiracy theory while here's more intimate and gradually turns to horror.
Since I don't want to spoil anything of the story all I'm saying is that the first playthrough took me almost four hours, horror elements are introduced without overdoing it (although some people may argue that they're kinda jump scares if the game hooks you like it happened to me it can be unsettling) and I think it's worth at least a second playthrough to get a different ending.

[i]Go for it if:[/i]

[*] you're curious about how text-adventures could evolve
[/list]

[i]Stay away if:[/i]

Simulacra is essentially a mixture of a horror-adventure and an epistolary novel. Its almost like an Alternate Reality Game, but it takes place in a fake internet, accessed through a fake cellphone. 

This is a very interesting method of depicting the story, and it comes with its own natural puzzle aspects that make it suited for a casual adventure game. 

The music is atmospheric. The plotline is pretty enjoyable, and believably written. Its creepy, and a good horror experience.

PROS
+ Atmospheric
+ Interesting presentation that has its own inherent mechanical aspects, thus making the gameplay feel natural
+ Very engaging

CONS
- Not a big challenge, nor the longest or deepest game out there.

OVERALL
An enjoyable casual horror-adventure. Atmospheric, creepy, and nicely presented. Absolutely recommended for fans of horror, fans of adventure games, fans of visual novels, and fans of experimental narrative games (aka "walking sims").

The list could go on and on. Although I enjoyed the game a lot, there are three minor things I'd like to mention, which I think could be better. 
The first is storywise. The story grows really great and creates so many expectations(especially because of the name "Simulacra"), but the ending is just not as strong as I expected. If you actually do know what this whole "Simulacra" thing is about(especially read the book Simulacra and Simulation by Jean Baudrillard), you just find the ending a little bit cheesy. No offense but, I think it could have been written way better. 
Secondly, the puzzles could be a little harder, just a little bit. I am aware that with this, it does not get in front of the story but you just expect one or two puzzles that could really challenge you. Yet, there is none. 
Lastly(this is a bit spoiler do not read this part unless you played it), I think it could have been better if the game also included the possibility of making the player believe or think that the whole plot could actually be a kidnapping(by Greg or Taylor) because I think, this would really improve the game. With no consideration of possible kidnapping scenarios, some dialogue options are so dead to choose(like you never believe that Taylor or Greg are somehow involved, so you are unlikely to accuse them).
These are just my humble opinions, nonetheless, I enjoyed the game a LOT! Thanks to anyone who were involved in creating this beautiful game. A great experience, nicely done!

What impressed me most was the way it breaks the fourth wall. Let me explain. Nowadays a lot of games engage in some kind of meta-commentary, be it lampshading or just generally making jokes or winking at the player. When it's done competently, it can be somewhat amusing.

This game is fun and I recommend it -- it's a good way to kill a few hours and is a bargain even at full price. The interface is fun, the mystery is fun, the suspense and creepiness is fun. But there are some not-fun things.

* the jumpscares are just kind of pointless. There's no reason for them to exist, not even within the narrative itself. They ended up making me roll my eyes. The Game's scariest moments are the ones where you feel a slow dread due to the knowledge you've gained

* the story isn't thematically coherent. it doesn't know what it's trying to say. in the end it makes some claim about the fakeness of social media or w/e, but that's not really supported by the rest of the game, which spends a lot more time with the cause and effect of non-social media-related interactions. That makes the denouement feel dissatisfying, as a lot of stuff, like the conflict with the ex-boyfriend or the relationship with the best friend, feel like they could have been replaced with anything else and the story remain intact, which means they're just window dressing and not even that important. It feels disrespectful to the player and to the characters.

* the game has multiple endings but doesn't let you skip ahead when dialogue is playing! This is the most irritating oversight. I ended up pulling up Cheat Engine on second playthroughs so I could turn up the game's speed so I didn't have to wait so long for the chat bubbles to show up. 

* dialogue looks like it was written by non-native English speakers, and I don't just mean text speak, I mean grammar wise it's awkward. Could stand to see some copy editing.

* just generally a lot of interesting concepts and ideas that get raised but not carried out to their full potential. There's a lot here to like, but a lot of misses in execution. I liked the interface messing directly with the player that happens partway through the game, but then nothing ever comes of it. It could have been totally cut from the game and the story would remain unchanged, which is just a bummer.

But those are my gripes, I still had a fun time, so yeah, buy the game!

[i]Simulacra[/i] is a captivating puzzle-slash-detective-slash-horror-slash-social commentary game which is yours to enjoy for a delightfully economic entree fee.

So you found a phone on your doorstep and it appears to belong to the now missing twenty-something Anna. Your quest to find out what happened to her will take place entirely through the smartphone interface, trying to get into contact with her familiars, sifting through her social media posts and recovering lost files. Soon enough the mysteries start to pile up. Those who have a basic grasp of the philosophy of Jean Baudrillard may already guess what's behind the sudden disappearance.

It's a short game which will take approximately 4-5 hours to finish, which is enough to get involved with the characters while still short enough so that the gameplay does not grow stale. There is replay value to be had, since your decisions (who to trust, what to do) can take the story to different conclusions.

The game touches on a few social issues, such as [spoiler]sexual harassment[/spoiler], [spoiler]the banality of social media content[/spoiler] and [spoiler]the ongoing digitization of society[/spoiler], but I never found the game to be either too preachy or too political. There is also some existential philosophy woven into the dialogues, though it's enough to give you something to muse about, it's too little to be considered profound. The puzzles are fairly easy, making the game more appealing to casual gamers rather than seasoned point-and-click fanatics.

At the bottom of all its qualities are certainly the jump scares. While it can be argued that this much loathed trope does the trick (i.e.: keeping you on edge even during the quiet moments), they are still a cheap substitute for the subtleties of psychological horror. That said, the game did manage to frighten me through the sheer eeriness of a digital device continually distorting into absolute madness, but the rather bland acting in the audio/video files often pulled me out of suspense-belief and back into the comfort zone.

[b][u]Final verdict:[/u] 7/10[/b]. [i]Simulacra[/i] is a fresh and well-executed, though somewhat poorly acted missing person mystery.

Since we are talking about a "mobile game port" (to my knowledge that is), there are some essentials lacking.

This game features no settings menu of any kind.
It is not possible to lower the audio, except through the OS' sound mixer ...
That is not acceptable, far less in a post TB (TotalBiscuit) world.
Being able to lower Sound, Music and/or Video (which is sparsely used), would make this a more proper PC-game.
Also I haven't seen the possibility to change resolution, though the game is played only on about 10% of the screen anyway (due to the type of game it is ...)

There are subtitles hidden in the help-menu in main menu.

Especially in the later part of the game, the music is a tad too loud in comparison with the voices, so understanding suffers from it.

Other than the just stated? Not much to complain about.
Scrolling is a bit awkward, but works well enough by mousewheel and "dragging" via left click.
Typing in the places necessary is a bit lackluster since backspace deletes the whole last word (which can be a pain for fast typers that want to correct a misstype ...)
